newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-WMC undaunted by lower profit.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-WMC undaunted by lower profit.

text.p: Australian gold and base metals miner WMC Ltd on Wednesday unveiled a widely anticipated fall in half-year profit but said an improvement in commodity prices and favourable exchange rates would see a second-half recovery.

The company reported an equity net profit for the six months to December 31 of A$100.7 million, a fall of 45.9 percent from a year ago. It attributed the slide to low commodity prices and a higher Australian dollar.
"The bottom line is where the company had talked the result down to," said a Melbourne-based analyst.
WMC had repeatedly warned of a weak first half.
But asked by reporters how the company's second half would compare with the first, WMC managing director Hugh Morgan said: "Markedly better."
He forecast higher nickel prices and a more favourable exchange rate, as well as higher production and lower costs.
The market, which had pummelled WMC's stock in the lead-up to the announcement, took the news well.
The shares leapt 18 cents before settling at A$7.95, up 13 cents on Tuesday's close.
Analysts said that despite the disappointment of the first half, the global metals cycle was on the mend and investors were punting on better times ahead.
"I think the market will say: 'Bad half, it's behind us. The reality is now that metals are moving, therefore the profits should be up'," said Prudential-Bache Securities analyst Tony Robson.
He rated the stock a buy. "Effectively you're buying in at the trough in profits."
Another analyst agreed: "Personally I have a very positive outlook on the stock. I think the second half numbers will be a lot better."
But analysts were troubled by nickel division earnings, which more than halved to A$64.4 million.
"The only really disappointing thing in the whole release was nickel which did particularly poorly," Robson said.

WMC blamed the slump on substantially lower realised nickel prices and a strong Australian dollar which offset a rise in production. The nickel division was also hit by an A$8.4 million workforce restrucuring charge.
However, WMC's Morgan was confident nickel production costs per unit would be cut by 10 percent by the company's year-end.
"We should get our 10 percent reduction by the 30th of June," Morgan told a news conference.
WMC announced the cost-cutting target late last year, but analysts have been sceptical about WMC's ability to meet it.
Morgan said the company had accelerated the expansion of its giant Olympic Dam copper, uranium, gold and silver project in South Australia.
The expansion, which aims to double copper output at the mine, has been brought forward about a year to 1999 and now carries a total capital cost of A$1.48 billion.
The expansion was initially costed at A$1.25 billion.
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1435
